title: Magnets and electromagnets
description: Animated KS3 Physics lesson on magnets for ages 9 to 14: north and south poles, magnetic materials, attract and repel, magnetic fields and field lines, compasses and the Earth's magnetic field, electromagnets and their uses.
intro: Poles, magnetic materials, field lines, compasses, electromagnets and how we use them, explained by the owl in six short parts.

steps.say: This is a bar magnet. Its two ends are called **poles**: a **north pole** and a **south pole**.
The magnetic force is strongest at the poles. See how the paper clips cling to the ends, not the middle.
Magnets attract **magnetic materials**. The magnetic metals are **iron**, **nickel** and **cobalt**. Most steel is magnetic too, because it is mostly iron.
Most other metals are **not** magnetic: copper, aluminium and gold stay put. So do wood and plastic.

check.q: Which of these is attracted to a magnet?
check.hint: Only a few metals are magnetic. Remember the three: iron, nickel and cobalt.
check.explain: **Iron** is a magnetic material, so the nail is pulled to the magnet. Copper, aluminium and gold are metals, but they are not magnetic.

steps.say: Bring two magnets close. A north pole and a south pole pull together: **opposite poles attract**.
Two north poles push each other apart. So do two south poles: **like poles repel**.
Magnetism is a **non-contact force**. The magnet pulls the paper clip up across the gap, without touching it.
Cut a magnet in half and you get two smaller magnets. Each half has its own north pole and south pole.

check.q: The north pole of one magnet is held near the north pole of another. What happens?
check.hint: Are the two poles the same (like) or different (opposite)?
check.explain: North and north are **like poles**, and like poles **repel**. Only opposite poles, north and south, attract.

steps.say: Around every magnet is a **magnetic field**. It is the space where the magnet pushes or pulls on magnetic things.
Sprinkle iron filings round a magnet and they line up in a pattern of curved lines.
We draw the pattern as **field lines**. Outside the magnet, the arrows always go from the **north pole** to the **south pole**.
The lines are closest together at the poles. That is where the field is **strongest**.
A small **plotting compass** points along the field lines, so you can use one to map a magnet's field.

check.q: Outside a bar magnet, which way do the field lines point?
options: From the north pole to the south pole
From the south pole to the north pole
From the middle out to both ends
check.hint: Think N to S, like reading the letters in "North to South".
check.explain: Outside a magnet the field lines go **from north to south**. A plotting compass shows the direction: its north end points along the line.

steps.say: A **compass** needle is a tiny magnet that can spin freely. Wherever you stand, it settles pointing north.
That's because the Earth has a **magnetic field**, a bit like a giant bar magnet inside it.
The compass needle lines up with the Earth's field, so its north end points towards the North Pole.
Here's a twist! Opposite poles attract, so the Earth's magnet must have its **south** pole up near the Arctic. That's what pulls the north end of the needle.

check.q: Why does a compass needle point north?
options: It lines up with the Earth's magnetic field
The North Pole is made of iron
check.hint: The needle is a small magnet. What is all around us that a magnet can line up with?
check.explain: The Earth has a **magnetic field**. The compass needle is a small magnet, so it lines up with the field and its north end points north.

steps.say: An electric **current** flowing in a wire makes a magnetic field around the wire. Look how the compasses turn.
Wind the wire into a **coil** and the field is stronger. It has the same shape as a bar magnet's field.
Put an **iron core** inside the coil and the field gets much stronger. Now it is an **electromagnet**.
Switch the current off and the magnetism stops. The paper clips drop!
To make an electromagnet stronger, use **more turns** of wire, a **bigger current**, or an **iron core**.

check.hint: Three things make it stronger: more turns, a bigger current and an iron core. Which option is the opposite of one of those?
check.explain: More turns make a stronger field, so **fewer turns** make it weaker. A bigger current and an iron core both make it stronger.

steps.say: The best thing about an electromagnet is that you can switch it **on** and **off**.
A scrapyard crane uses a huge electromagnet to lift old cars. Switch it off and the car drops.
In an **electric bell**, the electromagnet pulls an iron arm and the hammer hits the bell. This breaks the circuit, the arm springs back, and it all starts again.
Electromagnets are also in loudspeakers, electric door locks and the scanners used in hospitals.

check.q: Why does a scrapyard crane use an electromagnet instead of an ordinary magnet?
options: It can be switched off to drop the metal
It can pick up every metal, even aluminium
check.hint: What can an electromagnet do that a normal magnet can't?
check.explain: An electromagnet only works while the current is on. **Switch it off and the metal drops.** An ordinary magnet would never let go. (Neither kind can lift aluminium.)
